title: A Personalised Cancer Vaccine Just Kept Melanoma Away for Five Years. The Technology Could Reach South Asians Next.
excerpt: Moderna and Merck’s mRNA shot cut recurrence risk by 49 per cent and distant spread by 59 per cent — the longest follow-up ever for a personalised cancer vaccine. Nine more trials are under way.
body:
Five years ago, 157 people with aggressive melanoma entered a clinical trial that would test an idea straight out of science fiction: a vaccine custom-built from the molecular fingerprint of their own tumour, designed to teach their immune system to hunt down and destroy cancer cells before they could return.

This month, at the American Society of Clinical Oncology annual meeting in Chicago, the results came in. The combination of Moderna’s mRNA-based shot — intismeran autogene — with Merck’s blockbuster immunotherapy drug Keytruda reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 49 per cent compared to Keytruda alone. The risk of the cancer spreading to distant organs dropped by 59 per cent. And in an exploratory analysis, overall survival improved by 53 per cent.

The numbers, published simultaneously in ASCO’s *Journal of Clinical Oncology*, represent the longest follow-up data ever reported for a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine. They arrive at a moment when mRNA technology faces a strange paradox: celebrated in laboratories, embattled in politics.

## How It Works

Unlike traditional vaccines that target viruses, intismeran autogene is built from scratch for each patient. After a tumour is surgically removed, its DNA is sequenced to identify up to 34 unique mutations — neoantigens — that exist only on that patient’s cancer cells. An mRNA molecule encoding those neoantigens is then manufactured and injected, instructing the patient’s own cells to produce tiny fragments of the tumour proteins. The immune system recognises these fragments as foreign and mounts a targeted attack.

The entire process, from biopsy to injection, takes roughly six weeks. Each dose is a one-off, never to be repeated for another patient.

“That principle — teaching the immune system to recognise and attack a specific target — can now be applied to cancer, and that’s a big advance,” Merck Chief Medical Officer Eliav Barr said.

## A Pipeline, Not a Single Drug

The melanoma data is the tip of a far larger programme. Moderna and Merck are running nine active clinical trials of mRNA-based cancer therapies across lung, kidney, bladder, and pancreatic cancers. More than 130 mRNA-related studies were presented at ASCO this month alone.

Elsewhere, BioNTech and Roche are advancing their own mRNA cancer programmes. And just last week, Moderna received UK regulatory approval to begin a Phase 1/2 trial of an mRNA vaccine designed to *prevent* cancer in people with Lynch syndrome, an inherited condition affecting one in 300 people that dramatically raises the risk of colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancers.

Market research firm Vision Research Reports forecasts the personalised cancer vaccine market could reach $8.5 billion annually by 2034.

Jefferies analysts expect intismeran autogene to reach the market by 2027, with peak sales in the billions. The Phase 3 confirmatory trial in melanoma, INTerpath-001, is expected to deliver interim data next year.

## The Political Headwind

These advances unfold against an uncomfortable backdrop. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been openly sceptical of mRNA technology, and in August 2025 cancelled more than 20 government-funded mRNA vaccine contracts. Moderna was forced to discontinue three vaccine candidates in November 2025.

Yet the science continues to deliver. The five-year safety data showed no grade 4 or 5 adverse events. The most common side effects — fatigue, injection-site pain, and chills — were overwhelmingly mild.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

Melanoma rates among South Asians are lower than in lighter-skinned populations, but the cancers that do occur tend to be diagnosed later and at more advanced stages. Acral melanoma — found on the palms, soles, and nail beds — is disproportionately common in people with darker skin and carries a worse prognosis precisely because it is often missed.

But the larger significance of the mRNA platform lies beyond melanoma. If personalised cancer vaccines work — and five years of data now suggest they do — the same approach could eventually be applied to the cancers that devastate South Asian communities: gallbladder cancer, oral cancer, cervical cancer, and the gastric cancers that remain stubbornly common across the subcontinent.

For now, the technology remains expensive, logistically complex, and limited to clinical trials. But the trajectory is clear. The first cancer vaccine that works like a cancer vaccine is no longer theoretical. It has five years of data behind it.
